title: Adaptive Auto-Harness: Sustained Self-Improvement for Agentic System Deployment on Open-Ended Task Streams
authors: Zewen Liu, Zhan Shi, Yisi Sang, Bing He, Minhua Lin, Tianxin Wei, Dakuo Wang, Benoit Dumoulin, Wei Jin, Hanqing Lu
abstract: Agentic systems deployed in real-world scenarios face dynamic environments and open-ended task streams, where an initial, static model quickly becomes outdated. Existing approaches often rely on human feedback or carefully curated datasets for fine-tuning, which are costly, slow, and cannot keep pace with continuous changes. We introduce Adaptive Auto-Harness (AAH), a novel framework for sustained self-improvement of agentic systems on open-ended task streams. AAH operates through an iterative cycle: it (1) automatically generates diverse, challenging tasks reflective of current operational needs, (2) uses an innovative self-evaluation mechanism to identify limitations and failure modes of the current agent, and (3) leverages a powerful self-refinement module to generate improved agentic policies without human intervention. A key innovation of AAH is its adaptive task generation and self-evaluation, which dynamically adjust to the evolving capabilities of the agent and the characteristics of the task stream, preventing stagnation and ensuring continuous growth. We validate AAH on a suite of complex, open-ended agentic benchmarks, demonstrating its ability to significantly outperform static baselines and human-supervised fine-tuning methods in terms of robustness, adaptability, and long-term performance across diverse and continuously evolving task distributions. Our results highlight the potential of AAH to enable truly autonomous and self-improving agentic systems capable of indefinite operation in dynamic real-world environments.
paper_id: adaptive auto-harness: sustained self-improvement for agentic system deployment on open-ended task streams

title: Benchmarking Security Risk Detection and Verification in Open Agentic Skill Ecosystems
authors: Ismail Hossain, Sai Puppala, Zhuoran Lu, Sajedul Talukder, Nan Jiang
abstract: The rapid evolution of open agentic skill ecosystems, where autonomous agents dynamically discover, integrate, and execute skills from diverse, untrusted sources, introduces unprecedented security challenges. This paper presents a comprehensive benchmarking framework designed to evaluate the efficacy of security risk detection and verification mechanisms within these ecosystems. We categorize potential risks into several dimensions, including malicious skill injection, data leakage, privilege escalation, denial-of-service, and integrity violations, specifically tailored for the unique characteristics of skill-based interactions. Our framework comprises a novel dataset of both benign and intentionally vulnerable skills, spanning various functionalities and programming paradigms commonly found in open ecosystems. We propose a suite of quantitative metrics to assess the precision, recall, F1-score, and latency of security analysis tools, alongside qualitative measures for explainability and actionable insights. Through extensive experimentation with state-of-the-art static analysis, dynamic analysis, and machine learning-based detection techniques, we identify critical vulnerabilities and performance bottlenecks in existing approaches. The findings highlight the significant gap between current security tools and the complex, dynamic nature of open agentic skill ecosystems, underscoring the urgent need for more robust, scalable, and intelligent security solutions that can adapt to evolving threats and maintain trust in these decentralized environments.
paper_id: benchmarking security risk detection and verification in open agentic skill ecosystems

title: Resolution-Aware Perpetual Futures on Binary Prediction Markets: An Empirical Risk-Design Framework Using Polymarket Data
abstract: We develop and counterfactually evaluate a resolution-aware risk-design framework (PIRAP) for perpetual futures whose underlying tracks a single binary prediction-market probability through resolution. The framework specifies six components: an index estimator combining mid-price, depth-weighted mid, and time-decayed VWAP; jump-aware tiered margin sized against bounded-event terminal-collapse magnitude; leverage compression schedule contracting toward resolution; resolution-aware funding rule with boundary-aware correction; a multi-stage halt protocol; and an eligibility framework. Two formal non-portability propositions establish that standard basis-only funding paired with continuous-vol static margin fails on bounded-event underlyings. Empirical evaluation uses Polymarket's PMXT v2 archive for 2026-04-21 to 2026-04-27 (13,298-market analysis sample passing adequacy gates from 61,087 ingested; 13,115 resolved within the empirical window for E3). E1 evaluates two pre-registered stylized facts; E2 conducts counterfactual replay across three engine configurations; E3 isolates the resolution-zone protocol's contribution. Results are mixed. Five pre-registered floors: stylized-fact floors (boundary depth asymmetry, terminal-jump magnitude) PASS; welfare-side directional floors (final-hour liquidation -6%, drawdown -5.1% pooled, median PnL +14%) two FAIL one PASS; E3 mechanic floors (final-hour liquidation -80% by halt construction PASS; bad-debt frequency +2.4% FAIL). Three of five materiality floors fail: the framework as specified does not validate deployment, but the empirical record establishes a halt-versus-margin scope distinction (halt addresses execution-channel risk; terminal-jump bad-debt remains margin-side) and documents a pre-emption trade-off constraining the dynamic-margin component. The paper concludes with structural recommendations and explicit non-deployable status.

title: Who Wins and Who Loses In Prediction Markets? Evidence from Polymarket
authors: Pat Akey, Vincent Gregoire, Nicolas Harvie, Charles Martineau
abstract: We study trading gains and losses on Polymarket, the world’s largest prediction market platform. Our comprehensive dataset spans 2022 to 2026, covering more than 2.4 million users, $67 billion in volume, and 588 million trades. We document a striking profit concentration: the top 1% of users capture 76.5% of all trading gains. Despite this concentration, prices are well-calibrated and aggregate information efficiently. Gains flow almost entirely to sophisticated traders who trade using limit orders at prices that are advantageous relative to realized outcomes. Losses, by contrast, are associated primarily with liquidity-taking; longshot betting (trading at extreme prices) is a descriptive marker of losers but plays a smaller role once we control for activity scale. For roughly one in five losers, the lower-bound cost of taking liquidity alone is enough to flip their PnL from negative to positive. Monthly performance is only weakly persistent, however, so this cross-sectional pattern may reflect heterogeneous trading conditions or selection rather than persistent skill. Our results suggest that the informational benefits of prediction markets come at a cost to unsophisticated participants.

title: What Is the Alpha on Polymarket? A Methodology of Probability Mispricing and a Taxonomy of Eleven Profitable Regimes
abstract: A companion to "Smart Money on Polymarket" (Paper I), this paper asks a sharper, methodological question: what is the alpha? We argue and document that every profitable wallet in our N = 273 panel is running the same underlying strategy-probability mispricing arbitrage-differing only in (i) which part of the price spectrum the mispricing lives, and (ii) what generates it. We formalise the unifying framework, decompose the eleven empirical regimes documented in Paper I onto four alpha sources-slow information assimilation, behavioural biases, microstructure inefficiency, and cross-market inconsistency-and show that aggregate profits map cleanly onto these sources. The slow-information bucket alone accounts for ∼ $140M of the $177M total realised PnL in our panel, dominated by Politics specialists holding underpriced high-probability YES shares to a $1 resolution payoff. Behavioural-bias arbitrage (long-shot, contrarian) is small in absolute PnL but the highest-Sharpe bucket. Microstructure (HFT/MM) and cross-market (sports model, weather model) buckets contribute moderately. The single useful insight for a practitioner is unambiguous: Polymarket is not a casino and not a high-frequency arbitrage venue; it is a venue where positive expected value comes exclusively from being correctly contrarian to a measurable mispricing in the implied-probability surface.

title: The Anatomy of a Blockchain Prediction Market: Polymarket in the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
abstract: Using on-chain Polygon data, we analyze Polymarket's 2024 U.S. Presidential Election market and develop a transaction-level accounting framework with two components: a volume decomposition that separates exchange-equivalent turnover from share minting and burning, and trader-level disagreement measures. Naive aggregation reports $958M of October Trump-market volume, compared with $391M under our decomposition. Market quality improved as arbitrage-deviation half-lives fell from hours to under a minute and Kyle's&nbsp;λ dropped from 0.53 to 0.01. During October's large-account episode, capital flowed into both sides simultaneously, consistent with heterogeneous-beliefs trading rather than one-sided manipulation. The framework generalizes to other tokenized prediction markets.

title: The Polymarket Paradox: Manipulation, Whale Concentration, and Predictive Accuracy in the World's Largest Prediction Market
abstract: Polymarket processed roughly nine billion dollars in trading volume during 2024 and over three point seven billion dollars on the single 2024 US Presidential Election market alone. The platform produced a final election eve probability of fifty seven percent for Donald Trump that scored a Brier loss of zero point one eight five against an outcome that polling aggregates assigned roughly fifty fifty. It also hosted, simultaneously, the largest documented price impact event in prediction market history. A single French trader operating eleven linked wallets accumulated roughly eighty five million dollars in profit through concentrated directional bets, pushing the Polymarket Trump probability ten to fifteen percentage points above competitor platforms during October. Two oracle resolution disputes in 2025 saw markets totaling more than two hundred and fifty million dollars settle through governance votes that traders alleged were captured by token whales. These facts coexist uncomfortably. We document this paradox using verified anchor probabilities across five episodes spanning June 2024 to July 2025 and ten resolved binary markets for which we have election eve probability anchors directly verifiable in the public record. Polymarket assigned at least fifty percent probability to the eventual winner in seven of ten resolved markets, including six of eight battleground states. Mean Brier score across the ten was zero point two one three, with the headline presidential market at zero point one eight five. Yet the same data show that on individual episodes a single trader could move the headline price by ten percentage points or more, and that the resolution layer was not robust to capital concentration. We argue this is not a contradiction but a feature of the platform's information aggregation mechanism: counter parties have a profit incentive to take the other side of distorted prices, which corrects the average even while leaving individual prints distorted. We document the boundary conditions under which the correction works, where it fails, and what the limits of the platform's claim to be a reliable forecasting tool actually are.

title: Exploiting Mean-Reversion in Decentralized Prediction Markets: Evidence from Polymarket Binary Contracts
abstract: This study examines the profitability of mean-reversion trading strategies applied to binary outcome contracts on Polymarket, the world's largest decentralized prediction market platform. We analyze three distinct contracts representing varying risk profiles: a quasi-risk-free instrument (No to "Will Jesus Christ return in 2025?") and two high-yield speculative contracts (No to "Will China invade Taiwan in 2025?" and "Will the US confirm that aliens exist in 2025?"). Using high-frequency price data sampled at 10-minute intervals over approximately one year, we implement a parameterized mean-reversion framework across twelve strategy variants, testing robustness under varying liquidity constraints and transaction cost assumptions. Our findings reveal that while mean-reversion signals generate substantial alpha under passive limit-order execution (zero-spread scenario), strategy performance degrades significantly when more aggressive market orders are accounted for.

title: Kalshi and the Rise of Macro Markets
authors: Anthony M. Diercks, Jared Dean Katz, Jonathan H. Wright
abstract: This paper describes the economic and financial innovations that the prediction market platform Kalshi has introduced and considers the potential implications for monetary policy and macroeconomic stabilization. By making available markets that allow individuals to bet on the realization of a wide range of macroeconomic events and variables, Kalshi creates opportunities for new forms of hedging and and speculation. It may also provide a valuable source of information regarding expectations of future macroeconomic outcomes and the likely effects of policy interventions. The paper discusses various issues including the structure of Kalshi contracts, the mechanics of market operation, potential uses of these markets, and how they may be regulated.

title: Adverse Selection in Prediction Markets: Evidence from Kalshi
abstract: Using 41.6 million trades, we measure adverse selection in prediction markets. Adapting Kyle's λ and the Glosten-Harris decomposition, we show single-name markets exhibit greater informed price impact than broad-based markets. Despite this, effective spreads are only modestly wider, and market makers earn twice as much per contract. A frequency-magnitude decomposition resolves this puzzle: traders systematically overbet YES in markets that predominantly settle NO, generating a behavioral surplus that cross-subsidizes adverse selection. Adapting the VPIN toxicity metric, we find that one-sided order flow predicts maker losses in single-name markets but not broad-based markets. Our research suggests a new microstructure equilibrium concept for bilateral settlement markets.

title: Trend Quality and Predictability in Prediction Markets: Evidence from Minute-Level Kalshi Data
abstract: This paper studies whether "trend quality"-a drift-per-noise statistic computed from within-market price paths-predicts short-horizon price dynamics and ex-post forecast error in prediction markets. Using a large panel of minute-level Kalshi contract snapshots, we construct the Trend Quality Ratio (TQR), defined as the slope of a linear pre-close price trend normalized by its residual dispersion. In non-zero trend regimes, higher |TQR| is associated with both higher short-horizon directionality (continuation) and lower ex-post forecast error, with statistically significant differences between the top and bottom |TQR| deciles. Because many minute-sampled contracts exhibit zero post-window price change, we report both continuation rates conditional on non-zero movements and a tie-adjusted continuation score that retains zero-change cases. Midrange restrictions highlight the importance of bounded-price effects. Quotebased robustness using midquotes increases coverage in thinly traded contracts and preserves the strong error results, while directionality patterns are weaker and closer to 50% when prices are measured from quotes rather than trades.

title: Reconstructing Full Limit Order Books for Kalshi from WebSocket Streams
Convergence-Weighted Aggregation of Cross-Exchange Prediction Markets: A Dependency-Aware Index for Combining Prices Across Kalshi, Polymarket, Manifold, Metaculus, and Long-Tail Venues
abstract: Modern prediction-market venues — Kalshi, Polymarket, Manifold, Metaculus, and a long tail of newer exchanges — increasingly host overlapping markets on identical world events. Naive aggregation methods (simple or volume-weighted means, Hanson-style market-scoring averages, information-diversity weighted aggregators) treat each venue as a conditionally independent source given the resolution outcome. This assumption is violated in practice by three documented mechanisms: cross-exchange copy-trading bots, shared news flow that drives all venues simultaneously after material announcements, and arbitrageurs whose activity compresses cross-exchange variance below the level that would reflect genuine informational dispersion. Under this dependence, weighted-mean aggregators are biased and overconfident in the contamination regimes a deployer cares about most. We adapt the Index of Convergence Multi-epistemic (ICM) framework, originally developed for cross-disciplinary scientific aggregation (Stanisljevic, 2026), to the prediction-market setting. ICM augments naive aggregation with five components — agreement (A), direction (D), uncertainty overlap (U), perturbation invariance (C), and a dependency penalty (Pi) — yielding a convergence-weighted estimator that decouples genuine cross-source agreement from cross-source contagion. Within Pi, the lead-lag primitive Pi_L is the load-bearing component for the empirical bias-reduction result. We evaluate ICM-weighted aggregation against three baselines (naive mean, volume-weighted mean, Satopaa-Pemantle-Ungar logit-pool) on (i) synthetic experiments under each contamination mechanism in isolation, (ii) hybrid backtests with real Polymarket trajectories, and (iii) a strict cross-exchange backtest on binary markets where Polymarket and Manifold both have hourly history. Synthetic experiments confirm bias-reduction under copy-trading contamination (Mechanism I); the result is regime-targeted rather than uniformly dominant. The strict cross-exchange backtest is reported with the explicit caveat that ICM degenerates to the equal-weighted naive mean at V = 2 listing venues, so the reported Polymarket+Manifold result tests the surrounding pipeline but not the pair-discriminating ICM machinery. Forward-looking evaluation across additional exchanges (Kalshi via authenticated API, plus Metaculus and the long-tail venues) is planned with rolling collection commencing May 2026. Conjecture 1 (asymptotic bias reduction under contamination) is supported by a mechanism-by-mechanism heuristic argument; the formalization of the asymptotic-rate proof is left to follow-up.

title: Cryptocurrency Prediction Markets through the Derivatives Lens: Evidence from Kalshi and Polymarket
authors: Seungju Lee, Yebon Lee, Jaewook Lee
abstract: Cryptocurrency prediction markets have grown rapidly, yet their prices have been studied almost exclusively as probability forecasts. Because the binary contracts traded on these platforms are structurally identical to cash-or-nothing digital options, the standard derivatives pricing toolkit applies directly. We exploit this equivalence on 113,338 Bitcoin and Ethereum contracts traded on Kalshi and Polymarket between September 2025 and February 2026, extracting implied volatility surfaces, risk-neutral densities, and variance risk premia from prediction market prices for the first time. Risk-neutral skewness recovered from multi-strike Kalshi events is near zero, and the implied volatility smile is pronounced and roughly symmetric, contrasting with the persistent left-skewed smirk that crash-protection demand produces in equity index options. Implied variance exceeds realized variance across all contract series, documenting a positive variance risk premium in prediction markets. The VRP differs markedly across platforms, with Polymarket&apos;s roughly 16 times larger than Kalshi&apos;s, a pattern consistent with Polymarket&apos;s forward-start contract design, which anchors pre-window prices near 0.50 and inflates implied variance. Calibration analysis shows that both venues are systematically underconfident, with Polymarket exhibiting more severe probability distortion. A cross-platform comparison of matched contracts is consistent with much of this divergence reflecting the structural distinction between fixed-strike and forward-start contracts. The derivatives framework reveals risk pricing information in prediction markets that probability-based analysis alone cannot detect.

title: Makers and Takers: The Economics of the Kalshi Prediction Market
authors: Constantin Bürgi, Wanying Deng, Karl Whelan
abstract: This paper provides the first academic analysis of the economic characteristics of Kalshi, an event contract prediction market regulated by the CFTC. Kalshi is distinctive among prediction markets in allowing its users to act as market makers, providing liquidity by taking opposite sides of event contracts. We use a unique dataset of all trades on Kalshi between May 2021 and July 2022 to examine the market structure and the behaviour of its participants. We find that the average trading volume is surprisingly small, with 95% of contracts having less than 1,000 trades. The vast majority of trades occur for probabilities between 0.05 and 0.95, consistent with the market primarily serving hedging or speculative functions rather than pure information aggregation. We find that most traders specialize as either makers or takers, with only 12% switching roles over time. Takers are unprofitable on average, losing 11 cents per dollar traded. Makers are profitable on average, earning 7 cents per dollar traded. The largest 1% of maker accounts generate 90% of maker profits. A regression analysis shows that maker profitability is associated with taking the opposite side of taker trades that have lower initial stakes, suggesting makers exploit informational advantages over less committed takers. Finally, we analyse the speed of information processing using intraday data for trades on macroeconomic events. We find that event contract prices move rapidly in the direction of the underlying economic release, with most of the adjustment occurring within the first 10 seconds of the event.

title: Nous: An Attempt to Extract and Inject the Cognition Behind Prediction-Market Behavior
abstract: Prediction markets, such once-niche instruments, are growing in popularity due to their demonstrated accuracy in forecasting real-world events. However, their full potential remains untapped, largely due to the "wisdom of the crowd" effect, which averages away individual predictive nuances and biases. While this averaging yields superior aggregate predictions, it simultaneously obscures the intricate, often non-obvious cognitive processes underpinning individual trader behavior—the 'nous' behind their actions. This paper proposes a novel framework designed to explicitly extract these hidden cognitive models and, subsequently, inject them into new or existing prediction market scenarios. We introduce a methodology that combines deep learning techniques with causal inference to dissect individual trading decisions, identifying the latent factors (e.g., risk perception, information weighting, belief updating mechanisms) that drive their predictions. By analyzing a rich dataset of historical trades and associated market commentary, we construct probabilistic cognitive profiles for individual participants. Crucially, these profiles are not static; they are designed to be dynamically updated as new data becomes available. The "injection" component of our framework involves simulating the behavior of these extracted cognitive models within hypothetical or evolving market conditions. This allows for: 1) stress-testing market designs, 2) understanding potential emergent behaviors from specific cognitive mixes, and 3) augmenting nascent markets with synthetic, cognitively-informed agents to improve liquidity and information aggregation. Our preliminary results, using a synthetic market and a limited real-world dataset, demonstrate the feasibility of extracting meaningful cognitive patterns and show promising avenues for generating realistic, cognitively-driven market simulations. This work aims to move beyond merely aggregating predictions, towards understanding and actively leveraging the rich cognitive substrate of prediction markets.

title: Prediction Markets? The Accuracy and Efficiency of Political Prediction Markets in the 2024 Presidential Election
abstract: This paper investigates the accuracy and informational efficiency of political prediction markets in forecasting the 2024 United States Presidential Election. Drawing data from prominent market platforms, we critically assess how well market-derived probabilities align with actual election outcomes and benchmark their performance against traditional polling aggregates. Furthermore, we analyze the speed and extent to which these markets integrate new information, such as campaign developments, debate performances, and economic shifts, into their pricing mechanisms. Our analysis aims to determine whether prediction markets serve as a superior or merely complementary forecasting instrument to conventional methodologies, identifying potential sources of bias, overconfidence, or efficiency lags. The findings contribute to the broader understanding of collective intelligence and its application in political forecasting.
paper_id: prediction markets? the accuracy and efficiency of political prediction markets in the 2024 presidential election

title: WorldReasoner: Evaluating Whether Language Model Agents Forecast Events with Valid Reasoning
authors: Yizhou Chi, Eric Chamoun, Zifeng Ding, Andreas Vlachos
abstract: Forecasting future events requires not only accurate predictions but also valid reasoning behind those predictions. Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across many tasks, including event forecasting. However, it remains an open question whether their reasoning processes align with human understanding of validity. In this paper, we introduce WorldReasoner, a benchmark designed to evaluate the validity of reasoning provided by LLM agents for forecasting future events. WorldReasoner consists of 250 real-world scenarios, each with an event that has occurred and two alternative future events, only one of which actually happened. For each scenario, we collected human-written forecasts with reasoning, providing a gold standard for valid reasoning. Our evaluation framework goes beyond traditional accuracy metrics, focusing on three key aspects of reasoning validity: Coherence (internal consistency), Plausibility (alignment with common sense and background knowledge), and Non-Triviality (avoidance of obvious or uninformative statements). We benchmark several state-of-the-art LLMs, including GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, under various prompting strategies. Our findings reveal that while LLMs achieve reasonable forecasting accuracy, their reasoning often lacks crucial aspects of validity. Specifically, we observe that LLMs tend to struggle with providing non-trivial and truly insightful reasoning, frequently producing generic or overly cautious explanations. This work highlights the need for developing LLMs that can not only predict accurately but also articulate their predictions with robust and human-aligned reasoning.
paper_id: worldreasoner: evaluating whether language model agents forecast events with valid reasoning

title: Building Social World Models with Large Language Models
authors: Haofei Yu, Yining Zhao, Guanyu Lin, Jiaxuan You
abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated their impressive capabilities in generating human-like text and reasoning over complex prompts. While LLMs excel at understanding and generating natural language, their ability to model the social world—the intricate web of relationships, intentions, beliefs, and interactions that govern human behavior—remains an active area of research. This paper explores the potential of LLMs to serve as foundational components for building social world models. We propose a framework where LLMs are leveraged to infer latent social states, predict multi-agent interactions, and simulate plausible future scenarios within complex social environments. Specifically, we investigate how LLMs can be prompted to reason about agents' goals, beliefs, and personality traits, and to generate coherent narratives of social dynamics. We present a series of experiments demonstrating LLMs' capacity to reconstruct social graphs, infer unobserved social ties, and anticipate emergent group behaviors across various social settings, including multi-player games and real-world human interactions described in text. Our findings suggest that with appropriate prompting strategies and fine-tuning techniques, LLMs can develop a sophisticated understanding of social causality and facilitate the creation of more robust and realistic social simulations, paving the way for advancements in areas such as artificial social intelligence, human-computer interaction, and computational social science.
paper_id: building social world models with large language models

title: Are Short-Horizon Crypto Prediction Markets Calibrated? Evidence from 209,000 Polymarket Contracts, and a Cautionary Note on Inference with Pooled Strategy Entries
abstract: We provide the first calibration evidence on a new and almost unstudied market type: five-minute, USDC-denominated up/down contracts on the crypto prediction-market venue Polymarket. Using 209,453 resolved contract entries across Bitcoin, Ether, Solana, and Dogecoin over late March to early May 2026, we find that, conditional on the entries selected by a set of automated trading strategies, market-implied probabilities track realized outcome frequencies closely: the mean implied probability (0.4327) equals the realized win frequency (0.4328), and the slope of realized outcomes on implied probability is 1.012. We then show that a naive analysis would wrongly report a statistically significant favorite-longshot bias. The 209,453 entries are placed by roughly 145 strategies on only 18,239 distinct contracts, so entries that share a contract share an outcome and are not independent. Under an iid bootstrap the slope can appear to lie entirely above one, but under contract-clustered, day-clustered, and day-block-bootstrap inference its confidence interval always includes one, and the bootstrap assigns a 21 percent probability to a slope at or below one. The apparent bias reverses across assets (Ether slope 0.978) and across periods (an earlier Bitcoin sample, slope 0.981), and an out-of-sample live pilot of 905 contracts is badly miscalibrated. We conclude that these markets are statistically indistinguishable from calibrated, that no favorite-longshot bias survives dependence-robust inference, and that calibration studies pooling many correlated algorithmic entries must cluster on the underlying event and report effective, not nominal, sample size.

title: Reinforcement Learning for LLM-based Event Forecasting
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for enhancing event forecasting through the integration of Reinforcement Learning (RL) with Large Language Models (LLMs). While LLMs have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language understanding and generation, their application to complex, multi-step reasoning tasks such as predictive analytics for events often faces limitations in capturing subtle causal relationships, temporal dynamics, and optimizing for specific prediction metrics. We propose an architecture where an LLM generates initial forecasts and explanations, which are then refined through an RL agent. The RL agent learns an optimal policy for adjusting the LLM's outputs based on real-world feedback, historical performance, and domain-specific reward signals. This approach leverages the LLM's vast knowledge base for initial hypothesis generation while utilizing RL's strength in sequential decision-making and optimization under uncertainty. Our methodology focuses on training the RL agent to identify and correct biases, incorporate new information dynamically, and improve the accuracy and timeliness of event predictions across various domains. Empirical results demonstrate that the RL-enhanced LLM outperforms standalone LLMs and traditional forecasting models, achieving significant improvements in F1-score and Brier score across several benchmark event forecasting datasets.
paper_id: reinforcement learning for llm-based event forecasting

title: What Prediction Markets Can See: Market Formation, Settlement Legibility, and the Geography of Tradable Uncertainty in Africa and Latin America
abstract: When and how do prediction markets take root in places like Africa and Latin America? This paper examines how prediction markets emerge outside of Western, developed contexts, focusing on two key conditions: market formation and settlement legibility. Drawing on interviews with market makers and traders, regulatory documents, and market data from prediction market platforms operating in Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, and Brazil, I find that market formation is crucially shaped by local socio-political knowledge and networks, which market makers leverage to create relevant and engaging prediction events. Furthermore, the legibility of settlement—the ability to definitively determine the outcome of a prediction—is not solely a function of data availability but is also deeply influenced by local institutional environments and information ecologies. These factors shape which events are tradable and how market makers verify outcomes, influencing the geography of tradable uncertainty. The paper contributes to the understanding of financial market development in emerging economies, the sociology of knowledge and expertise in markets, and the broader political economy of information.

title: EventConnector: Mining Social Event Relations through Temporal Graphs
authors: Zijie Lei, Haofei Yu, Ge Liu, Jiaxuan You
abstract: Social events, such as protests, concerts, or conferences, are fundamental to human society. Understanding the relationships between these events, such as one event being a precursor or a consequence of another, is crucial for gaining deeper insights into societal dynamics and for applications like event forecasting. However, mining these complex relations is challenging due to the sparse, temporal, and often implicit nature of the connections between events. Traditional approaches often rely on explicit mentions or direct links, overlooking the rich, indirect, and time-evolving dependencies. In this paper, we propose EventConnector, a novel framework for mining social event relations through temporal graphs. EventConnector first constructs a dynamic event graph where nodes represent events and edges capture various forms of interactions and dependencies over time. We introduce a new method for generating temporal edges based on shared context, co-occurrence patterns, and geographical proximity within specific time windows. To model the evolutionary nature of event relations, EventConnector employs a novel temporal graph neural network (TGNN) architecture that is designed to capture both short-term sequential dependencies and long-term structural patterns in the event graph. This TGNN learns continuous-time representations for events, which are then used to predict different types of relations (e.g., cause-effect, follow-up, related-to). We evaluate EventConnector on two real-world datasets of social events, demonstrating its superior performance in predicting event relations compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, we provide case studies that illustrate the interpretability of our model and its ability to uncover non-obvious social event dynamics.
paper_id: eventconnector: mining social event relations through temporal graphs

title: Toward a Geopolitical Crisis Observatory: Diagnosing Systemic Risk in News Flows Using Complex Systems Science
abstract: The world is currently experiencing an unprecedented convergence of geopolitical, economic, social, environmental, and technological crises, pushing global systems toward instability and potential tipping points. While early warning systems exist for specific hazards like financial crashes or natural disasters, a comprehensive, real-time observatory capable of diagnosing and forecasting systemic risks arising from the complex interplay of multiple geopolitical factors is still lacking. This paper outlines a conceptual framework for a "Geopolitical Crisis Observatory" leveraging advancements in complex systems science, artificial intelligence, and big data analytics. We propose to analyze vast streams of global news, social media, and open-source intelligence data as a proxy for the collective human perception and response to unfolding events. Drawing on methodologies developed for financial market analysis, earthquake forecasting, and critical phenomena, we aim to identify characteristic patterns of escalating tension, accelerating information cascades, and emerging systemic vulnerabilities within these data flows. Specifically, we discuss techniques such as self-organized criticality, early warning signals for critical transitions (e.g., rising variance, autocorrelation, and skewness), and network theory to map the evolving landscape of interconnected risks. The objective is not to predict specific events, but rather to detect the onset of critical phases where the system becomes highly susceptible to rapid, non-linear shifts and to provide actionable insights for decision-makers to mitigate the potential for widespread instability and conflict.
paper_id: toward a geopolitical crisis observatory: diagnosing systemic risk in news flows using complex systems science

title: Who Profits in Binary Prediction Markets? Maker-Taker Dynamics, Behavioral Bias, and Sentiment Arbitrage on Kalshi
abstract: Whether liquidity providers in binary prediction markets systematically profit from uninformed order flow, and whether behavioral biases sustain that profit, remain open empirical questions. We address them using 72.1 million executed trades ($18.3B notional) on Kalshi from July 2021 through November 2025, supplemented by 404.5 million on-chain trades from Polymarket, applying volume-weighted return decomposition, calibration analysis, OLS regression, and paired t-tests. A statistically significant Favorite-Longshot Bias (FLSB) emerges on both platforms, but with a cross-platform contrast: Kalshi longshots are overpriced (δ b &lt; 0, p &lt; 0.001 for all sub-25% buckets) while Polymarket favorites above 55% implied probability are systematically underpriced (δ b &gt; 0, t up to 361), implicating market design as the key moderating factor. On the supply side, makers earn +0.83 percentage points (pp) in volumeweighted returns (p = 0.0055), constituting a $142.5M wealth transfer that exceeds estimated bid-ask spread compensation by 0.13 pp. This alpha is not uniform: it ranges from +0.29 pp in Finance to +3.01 pp in World Events, with high-volume categories spanning +0.82 pp (Sports) to +1.78 pp (Media), consistent with adverse selection varying by information environment. On the demand side, takers allocate 63.8% of capital to YES contracts despite earning 0.32 pp less than NO-side takers, an affirmative framing bias unexplained by differential risk. Contrary to efficiency-convergence predictions, maker alpha trends upward at +8.21 bp/month (R 2 = 0.70) as retail participation grows. A sport-level decomposition of the dominant sports category (74% of volume) reveals maker alpha ranging from +0.18 pp in MLB to +3.43 pp in UFC/Boxing, with no significant time-to-resolution decay (p = 0.88), providing direct evidence of persistent fandriven sentiment arbitrage. Taken together, these findings indicate that binary prediction markets structurally disadvantage uninformed retail participants and call for targeted disclosure requirements and calibration-oriented regulatory oversight.

title: Underreaction, Salience, and Hot-Hand Beliefs in Sports Event-Contract Markets: Evidence from Kalshi NBA and NFL
authors: Jaewook Lee, Yebon Lee, Seungju Lee
abstract: Prediction markets are widely regarded as efficient aggregators of public information, yet how quickly their prices absorb that information, and whether the speed depends on how the information arrives, remains unsettled. In-play sports contracts let us examine this directly. Evolving game states yield an objective, second-by-second win-probability benchmark against which prices can be tracked trade by trade. We exploit this setting using 41.8 million transactions across 1,496 NBA and NFL games on Kalshi, matched to play-by-play benchmarks. In both sports, prices adjust to scoring news only gradually and incompletely within short post-event windows, a robust underreaction consistent with limited attention. The adjustment path tracks each sport&apos;s scoring structure. NBA prices drift steadily toward the benchmark after frequent, small shocks, whereas NFL prices settle at a flatter, less complete level after rarer, larger shocks. Salient, highlight-like events draw a weaker short-run response, most clearly in the NBA. Prices show no tendency to extrapolate scoring runs beyond fundamentals, leaving no role for hot-hand pricing. Although benchmark deviations exceed plausible fee-and-spread hurdles across the price distribution, a mean-reversion rule earns nothing net of costs. The market is inefficient in how fast it incorporates information, not in offering exploitable profit.

title: Preference Optimization Drives Monoculture in LLM Prediction Markets
authors: James Begin, Brendan Gho, Suman Muppavarapu, Tyson Tsay, Atharva Mohan, Afnan Shaik, R K Li, Vasu Sharma, Archana Vaidheeswaran
abstract: Preference optimization (PO) techniques, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), have been instrumental in aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences, significantly improving their performance across various tasks. However, the widespread adoption of these methods has led to a critical, under-examined consequence: the homogenization of LLM outputs, particularly when models are used in prediction markets or situations requiring diverse perspectives. In this paper, we explore how PO, by systematically rewarding responses that align with perceived optimal or common preferences, inadvertently drives LLMs towards a "monoculture" of predictions. Through a series of experiments using simulated prediction markets and real-world datasets, we demonstrate that PO-aligned models converge on highly similar predictions, reducing the diversity and robustness of collective intelligence, and potentially amplifying biases present in the preference data. We quantify this phenomenon by measuring the reduction in entropy of prediction distributions and the increased inter-model agreement after PO. Our findings suggest that while PO enhances individual model performance, it may undermine the benefits of ensemble diversity crucial for complex problem-solving and accurate forecasting in multi-agent systems. We discuss the implications of this monoculture for areas like scientific discovery, financial markets, and creative generation, and propose avenues for developing preference optimization techniques that balance alignment with the preservation or promotion of diverse outputs.

title: Forecasting With LLMs: Improved Generalization Through Feature Steering
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promise in time series forecasting, achieving state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. However, despite their successes, LLMs still suffer from poor generalization outside of training distributions, particularly when applied to new datasets or tasks. This limitation stems from the static nature of their internal feature representations, which are learned during pretraining and remain fixed during finetuning. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Feature Steering (FS) to improve the generalization of LLMs for forecasting tasks. FS introduces a lightweight, task-specific module that adaptively modulates the internal feature representations of the LLM based on the characteristics of the input time series. This allows the model to dynamically adjust its focus and leverage relevant features for different forecasting scenarios. We evaluate FS on a diverse set of real-world time series datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in generalization performance compared to traditional finetuning methods. Our results show that FS enhances the LLM's ability to adapt to unseen data patterns, leading to more robust and accurate forecasts. Furthermore, we provide interpretability analyses illustrating how FS dynamically influences the LLM's feature space, offering insights into its improved generalization capabilities.
paper_id: forecasting with llms: improved generalization through feature steering

title: Human Capital, Not Model Benchmarks, Predicts Hybrid Intelligence in Forecasting
abstract: This paper investigates the relative contributions of human versus artificial intelligence (AI) in forecasting tasks, particularly in the context of hybrid intelligence systems. Contrary to prevailing research that often prioritizes model performance metrics as predictors of overall system accuracy, we demonstrate that attributes of human capital—specifically, cognitive diversity and domain expertise within the human teams—are significantly more predictive of forecast accuracy than the benchmark performance of the underlying AI models. Through a series of forecasting experiments involving diverse human teams and various AI models, our findings suggest that the value added by sophisticated AI models is contingent upon, and often overshadowed by, the qualitative characteristics of the human forecasters. We argue for a re-evaluation of current approaches to hybrid intelligence system design, emphasizing the critical role of human team composition and capabilities over solely optimizing AI model benchmarks. This work has implications for understanding and designing more effective human-AI collaborative systems, particularly in complex and uncertain domains such as geopolitical forecasting or economic prediction.
paper_id: human capital, not model benchmarks, predicts hybrid intelligence in forecasting

title: Diverse Evidence, Better Forecasts: Multi-Agent Deliberation Under Information Asymmetry
authors: Yuante Li, Yicheng Tao, K Zhang, Taozhi Wang, G D Gu, Yaxin Zhou
abstract: Forecasting is essential for planning and decision-making in many domains. While there is a rich literature on single-agent forecasting, real-world forecasting often involves multiple agents with diverse information. How to aggregate information from these agents to produce accurate forecasts remains an open question. This paper introduces a multi-agent deliberation framework designed to leverage diverse evidence for improved forecasting under information asymmetry. Our framework, inspired by human deliberative processes, enables agents to exchange and synthesize information through structured communication rounds. We model the agents' internal reasoning and communication strategies using a combination of Bayesian inference and deep reinforcement learning, allowing them to learn optimal deliberation policies. Empirical evaluations across various simulated forecasting tasks demonstrate that our multi-agent deliberation framework significantly outperforms conventional aggregation methods and single-agent models, particularly in scenarios characterized by complex dependencies and partial information. We analyze the emergent communication strategies and show how agents learn to effectively share complementary information, mitigate individual biases, and refine their collective understanding of the underlying events. The results suggest that structured multi-agent deliberation can harness information diversity to produce more robust and accurate forecasts, offering a promising direction for designing intelligent forecasting systems.
paper_id: diverse evidence, better forecasts: multi-agent deliberation under information asymmetry

title: Settlement Manipulation in Prediction Markets
authors: David Dai, Ruizhe Jia, Shihao Yu
abstract: Prediction markets incentivize truthful reporting by rewarding agents for accurate predictions. However, the accuracy of agents' predictions is evaluated against a ground truth which is often determined by a settlement procedure rather than an immutable physical process. Such procedures are susceptible to manipulation, especially when they involve human discretion. This paper initiates the study of settlement manipulation in prediction markets. We model settlement manipulation as an agent's strategic choice to take an action that influences the settlement outcome of the market. We analyze the conditions under which manipulation occurs and quantify its severity. Our findings indicate that manipulation can be substantial even when the manipulator has a low stake in the market. We propose several mitigation strategies, including charging manipulators for the cost of their actions and penalizing them for large deviations from the true outcome. We provide theoretical guarantees on the effectiveness of these strategies in reducing manipulation. Finally, we empirically evaluate our strategies using real-world data from a prediction market on sports games, demonstrating their practical utility.

title: The Shape of Macroeconomic Beliefs
abstract: This paper studies the shape of macroeconomic beliefs held by households. I introduce a novel estimation method for the household subjective probability distribution of future inflation and output growth, based on categorical survey data. The method jointly estimates both the location and the shape of beliefs, relying on a flexible functional form (the Normal-Inverse Gaussian distribution) to capture departures from normality such as skewness and fat tails. Using monthly data from the Michigan Survey of Consumers, I find that households' subjective distributions are characterized by substantial time-varying skewness and fat tails. I show that both the mean and the shape of beliefs significantly predict household consumption and investment decisions, as well as their actual future spending. Furthermore, I find that the shape of beliefs is closely related to perceived macroeconomic uncertainty and captures the degree of disagreement among households. I conclude that understanding the shape of household beliefs is key to understanding and predicting their economic decisions.

title: The Limits of Prediction: A Comparative Analysis of Market Efficiency Across Three Kalshi Prediction Market Events (A Case Study in Forecasting Precision, Liquidity, and Information Incorporation)
abstract: This paper examines three distinct Kalshi prediction market events-the US PPI MoM release, the FOMC rate decision with dissent count, and the 10-year Treasury yield-to explore the relationship between event characteristics, market liquidity, and forecasting precision. We find that prediction markets exhibit varying degrees of efficiency depending on the nature of the underlying event, the availability of information, and the liquidity of the contract. The PPI market, with its scheduled release and clear consensus forecast, demonstrated the most gradual information incorporation. The FOMC contract, with its combination of policy decision and human judgment (dissents), exhibited noisy information flow and overestimation of dissent probability. The Treasury yield contract, with its thin liquidity and lack of a specific announcement time, showed the most dramatic late-stage repricing. These findings have implications for the design of prediction markets, the interpretation of their prices as probability estimates, and the limits of forecasting in financial markets.

title: Volatility in Prediction Markets: A Structural Approach
authors: Weiye Xi, Ciamac C. Moallemi, Mallesh Pai, Shouqiao Want
abstract: This paper proposes a structural framework to analyze volatility in prediction markets, focusing on how information aggregation and market design interact to shape price dynamics. We model a market where agents receive private signals about a future event and trade a contract whose payoff depends on the event's outcome. Our approach allows us to disentangle the impact of fundamental uncertainty from market-induced volatility, such as those arising from information cascades, strategic trading, or limited market participation. We derive theoretical results demonstrating how the precision of private signals, the number of market participants, and the market maker's rule affect price variance and convergence speed. Empirically, we test our model using data from real-world prediction markets, showing that our structural estimates can explain observed patterns of volatility and predict how changes in market parameters might alter market efficiency and informativeness. The findings offer insights into designing more robust and informative prediction markets.
paper_id: volatility in prediction markets: a structural approach

title: When do prophets profit in prediction markets?
authors: Anri Gu, Nicole Kagan, Alec Sun, Jibang Wu, Haifeng Xu
abstract: Prophets in prediction markets are agents that have early access to information about the outcome of an event. While it is well known that prophets are guaranteed to profit if they trade optimally in a standard continuous double auction market, this is not necessarily true when they trade against other agents using algorithmic strategies. We show that when prophets interact with zero-intelligence (ZI) agents, they are guaranteed to profit if and only if the event probability is an affine function of the signal value. If ZI agents use a linear pricing function, prophets are guaranteed to profit regardless of how the event probability depends on the signal value. We then show that against agents that learn the prophet's strategy, such as reinforcement learning agents, prophets cannot make a profit. Furthermore, even against learning agents, we show that simple strategies can allow the prophet to break even. Our findings provide insights into the conditions under which early information leads to profit and highlight the challenges prophets face against sophisticated algorithmic traders.
paper_id: when do prophets profit in prediction markets?

title: Beyond Forecasting: The Belief-to-Trade Layer in Prediction-Market Agents
authors: Yishu Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Jiaqi Deng, Hanyang Tang
abstract: Prediction markets have garnered significant interest as a distributed mechanism for aggregating private information. However, existing models for agents operating in these markets primarily focus on sophisticated forecasting strategies, often neglecting the crucial step of translating beliefs into concrete trading actions. This paper introduces the "Belief-to-Trade Layer," a novel conceptual and computational component designed to bridge this gap. We argue that an agent's trading strategy is not solely a function of its probabilistic forecasts but is also influenced by its risk preferences, capital constraints, perceived market liquidity, and strategic considerations regarding other agents. We propose a framework for modeling this layer, encompassing modules for risk assessment, utility maximization, and dynamic order generation. Through simulations with diverse agent types, we demonstrate that agents equipped with an explicit Belief-to-Trade Layer exhibit more realistic trading behaviors, achieve higher long-term utility, and contribute to more efficient market outcomes, even when their underlying forecasting capabilities are identical. Our findings suggest that future research in prediction market design and agent modeling should critically consider this often-overlooked intermediate layer for a more complete understanding of market dynamics and agent rationality.
paper_id: beyond forecasting: the belief-to-trade layer in prediction-market agents

title: Hindcast: Replaying Prediction Markets to Evaluate LLM Forecasters
authors: Xiao Ye, Jacob Dineen, Evan Zhu, S Lu, Kevin Song, Ben Zhou
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly demonstrating capabilities as forecasters, yet rigorously evaluating their forecasting prowess remains challenging. Existing benchmarks typically compare LLM predictions to ground truth, a method limited to evaluating events that have already transpired and do not require expert judgment to resolve. This approach fails to capture the full spectrum of a forecaster's utility, particularly in scenarios where the ground truth is subjective or unknowable, or where an early, accurate prediction is more valuable than a late, perfect one. To address these limitations, we introduce **Hindcast**, a novel evaluation framework that assesses LLM forecasters by replaying historical prediction markets. By treating LLMs as participants in these markets, Hindcast evaluates their ability to "buy low and sell high"—profitably trading on their predictions before events resolve. This market-based approach inherently weighs accuracy against timeliness and confidence, offering a more holistic and robust assessment than traditional methods. We demonstrate Hindcast's efficacy by evaluating various LLMs across 3,690 questions from over five years of forecasting data. Our findings show that even basic LLM prompts can generate profitable forecasts, and that the quality of these forecasts is correlated with LLM size. Notably, the best LLM forecasters approach the performance of top human forecasters, who consistently outperform market averages. Hindcast provides a powerful and flexible tool for developing and comparing LLM forecasting systems, paving the way for more sophisticated and practically relevant evaluations.
paper_id: hindcast: replaying prediction markets to evaluate llm forecasters

title: Prices, Probabilities, and Parlays: Systematic Bias in Sports Prediction Markets
abstract: This paper investigates the pricing of sports wagers and the predictability of betting market returns. We provide empirical evidence of systematic biases in the pricing of parlay bets, which are combinations of multiple individual wagers. By comparing the implied probabilities from individual wagers to the implied probabilities of parlay outcomes, we find that parlays are consistently overpriced relative to their component parts. This overpricing is robust across different sports and bet types, suggesting a systematic market inefficiency. We construct a profitable betting strategy by exploiting these mispricings, demonstrating that the market's pricing of complex wagers is not fully efficient. Our findings contribute to the literature on behavioral finance and market microstructure, highlighting potential cognitive biases among bettors or operational inefficiencies within the sports betting market that lead to predictable deviations from rational pricing.
paper_id: prices, probabilities, and parlays: systematic bias in sports prediction markets

title: WorldCupArena: Fine-Grained Evaluation of Language Models and Deep-Research Agents on Football Forecasting
authors: Zhaokai Wang, Tianlin Gui, Jiayuan Rao, Shangzhe Di, Yihong Tang, D Liang
abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated their impressive capabilities in general knowledge and reasoning tasks. However, their performance in dynamic, real-world scenarios requiring deep domain expertise and continuous knowledge acquisition remains underexplored. This paper introduces WorldCupArena, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs and deep-research agents on the challenging task of football match forecasting. WorldCupArena features a diverse dataset encompassing historical match data, team statistics, player information, and contextual factors relevant to major football tournaments, particularly the FIFA World Cup. Our fine-grained evaluation framework goes beyond simple win/loss prediction, assessing models on various aspects: predicting scorelines, analyzing tactical decisions, identifying key player performances, and providing coherent explanations for their forecasts. We evaluate several state-of-the-art LLMs and a custom-built deep-research agent leveraging advanced information retrieval and reasoning components. Our findings reveal that while LLMs possess strong foundational knowledge, they often struggle with the dynamic nature and intricate details of football, exhibiting limitations in real-time data integration, nuanced tactical understanding, and robust causal reasoning for specific match outcomes. The deep-research agent, by contrast, demonstrates superior performance, highlighting the critical role of specialized data processing, expert knowledge integration, and systematic research capabilities for high-stakes forecasting tasks. This work provides a comprehensive benchmark for future research in evaluating and improving AI systems for complex, dynamic, and knowledge-intensive domains.
paper_id: worldcuparena: fine-grained evaluation of language models and deep-research agents on football forecasting

title: Optimal Market Making in Prediction Markets
abstract: We study the problem of an optimal market maker in a prediction market that trades a contract whose value is determined by a future event. The market maker aims to maximize their expected terminal wealth under risk constraints, specifically using the Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). We model the market maker's problem as a continuous-time stochastic control problem in a general framework where the prediction market contract can be traded continuously. We derive the optimal market making strategy explicitly in a specific setup involving a geometric Brownian motion for the belief process. Our results show that the market maker's optimal strategy depends on their risk aversion, the size of their inventory, and the volatility of the underlying belief process. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of different risk aversion levels on the market maker's behavior, showing how higher risk aversion leads to more conservative strategies aimed at reducing inventory risk. Our findings provide theoretical insights into the dynamics of prediction markets and offer practical implications for designing automated market making algorithms.
paper_id: optimal market making in prediction markets

title: When Do Prediction Markets Resolve Uncertainty? Trading-Period Belief Variation and Resolution Jumps on Polymarket
abstract: Using a new keyset rerun based on Polymarket Gamma /markets/keyset, this paper measures from price processes when prediction markets resolve event uncertainty. By decomposing the price histories of binary event contracts into realized belief variation during trading and the resolution jump that remains at resolution, the paper describes the timing of uncertainty resolution that cannot be seen from price-level forecast accuracy alone. The normalized research universe contains 50,500 closed markets, from which a keyset sample of 12,000 markets is constructed. The baseline daily specification contains 10,376 markets and 25,640 market-horizon rows; mean RV trade is 0.0531, mean J resolution is 0.0567, and mean RV total is 0.1098. The stacked mean JumpShare is 0.3528, the median is 0.0876, and the mean TradeShare is 0.6472, indicating that the terminal component at resolution is not negligible. JumpShare, however, is a descriptive decomposition measure conditional on the horizon and frequency, not a market-specific structural parameter. At the 30-day horizon, mean JumpShare falls to 0.1623; at 12-hour and 6-hour frequencies it falls to 0.3067 and 0.1744, respectively. By event type, live_or_continuous has the highest JumpShare and one_touch_or_barrier the lowest. The coefficient on market volume is positive and statistically significant, and market_volume_total should be interpreted as a cumulative market size / attention proxy rather than as liquidity. The results suggest that both the evaluation of prediction markets and the design of event derivatives should explicitly account not only for continuous belief variance but also for terminal jump risk.

title: APMM: Automated Parlay Market Maker
authors: Niusha Moshrefi, Ranvir Rana, Pramod Viswanath
abstract: Parlay bets, a popular form of wager that combines multiple individual bets into a single, higher-payout bet, suffer from substantial inefficiencies due to human error and limited liquidity in traditional markets. We introduce APMM, an Automated Parlay Market Maker, designed to provide transparent, dynamic pricing and ensure liquidity for parlay bets across various events. Our system leverages a novel mathematical framework, extending concepts from existing automated market makers (AMMs) in decentralized finance, to efficiently price and manage risk for complex parlay structures. APMM employs a continuous product market maker model for individual legs and integrates a bespoke risk-hedging mechanism that dynamically adjusts payouts based on real-time probabilities and market demand. Through simulation and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that APMM can significantly improve price accuracy, reduce transaction costs, and enhance market depth compared to manual bookmaking, offering a more robust and accessible platform for parlay betting.
